thesis: This episode argues that The New York Times is a unique, human-curated digital subscription powerhouse with a massive engaged audience and a diversified portfolio that feeds itself, positioning it as a rare 'essential' company in the content space. It contrasts this with the dominance of tech giants like Netflix and Amazon, suggesting that while tech controls the media hegemony, The Times has successfully built a sustainable, high-margin business that is well-inside the market and likely to endure for a long time.

claims.claim: The New York Times is the largest first-party content company by subscriber count in the world and aims to be the essential subscription for curious people everywhere.
claims.quote: I would sort of describe it as you are the largest first-party content company by subscriber count in the world. I mean, what other... It's more than a newspaper now. Am I thinking about that right?

claims.claim: The New York Times is the fastest-growing audience on The Times due to the Athletic newsroom, and the whole portfolio feeds each other.
claims.quote: I talk about the size of that Athletic newsroom, and by the way, the Athletic audience is the fastest-growing audience on The Times. Because if you're a sports fan, where are you getting your really good, hardcore, in-the-locker-room sports journalism from?

claims.claim: The New York Times is a human-curated company and believes journalism is a human endeavor, not something AI can replace.
claims.quote: In the age of AI, it's interesting, right, that you are a human-curated company. Everything that The New York Times does is human-curated. Absolutely. But a lot of the people in this room, they turn to AI to do a lot of the things that you just described. And yet, business is going great.

claims.claim: The New York Times believes the law is on their side regarding the lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft for training without permission on New York Times content.
claims.quote: So that's one. We believe the law is on our side. And by the way, not just the side of journalism. This is not just an issue for news organizations, although that is a pretty important issue to society. This is an issue for anybody who makes creative work, anyone who makes IP.

claims.claim: The New York Times has a partnership with Amazon that provides sustainable, fair value exchange and gives The Times control over how its journalism and other content would be used.
claims.quote: And as we've done, we just did a partnership with Amazon, and we did that because we saw it as having sustainable, fair value exchange and giving The Times control over how its journalism and other content would be used.

claims.claim: The New York Times has put an enormous amount of effort and care and money and method into trying to reduce bias in every way they can.
claims.quote: And it's worth saying, because I do get asked about bias all the time on any topic, it's worth saying we put an enormous amount of effort and care and money and method into trying to reduce bias in every way we can. In the process, we have a giant standards operation that really says this is an okay source or this isn't.

claims.claim: The New York Times has lots of hit shows like The Daily, The Ezra Klein Show, and Interesting Times with Ross Douthat that are deepening engagement and making many new people love the Times.
claims.quote: We've got lots of hit shows: The Daily, The Ezra Klein Show, our new show, which is the New Right's answer to The Ezra Klein Show; "Interesting Times with Ross Douthat," and "Hard Fork," which I think is similar to you. What are those shows doing for us? One, they are deepening the engagement we have with people who already love the Times.

claims.claim: The company is the largest digital subscription newspaper in the world with a market cap of almost $10 billion.
claims.quote: And here, in the few short years since then, you are the largest digital subscription newspaper in the entire world. You are the only standalone global newspaper company left. Market cap of almost $10 billion, an all-time high.

claims.claim: The company has a huge engaged audience with 50 to 100 million people coming to the website and apps every week.
claims.quote: Every week now, 50 to 100 million people are coming to The Times website and apps. Some 20 million or so people listen to our podcasts and read our newsletters. We've got about 150 million people who've registered with us, and that number is still growing.

claims.claim: The newspaper is well inside 30% of the business, probably 20 to 25%, and will be around for a long time.
claims.quote: So, you asked me what's different now? I would say, one, print is... well, the newspaper is well inside of 30% of the business. We've got a huge engaged audience, as I just described. Wait, the physical newspaper is still almost 30% of the business? It's well inside. It's probably 20, 25%, but yeah, and by the way, it's going to be around a long time.

claims.claim: The company has expanded beyond news to include games, sports, Wirecutter, cooking, and recipes.
claims.quote: So what is the strategy then? You've expanded well beyond news: there are games, sports, Wirecutter, cooking, recipes. That means it's subscriptions to things beyond news.

claims.claim: Shopify powers various brands including Eastside Golf.
claims.quote: We're Eastside Golf, and we're powered by Shopify.

claims.claim: ServiceNow connects every corner of the business and puts AI to work for people.
claims.quote: Only ServiceNow connects every corner of your business, putting AI to work for people. Every corner. Every corner. Nick. So, Kate in HR can focus on people, not processing. Patti in IT is using AI agents to deal with the small stuff so she can work on the big stuff. AI helps Jim solve customer problems before they become problems.

claims.claim: The company was on the brink of death in 2008 and sold its headquarters building.
claims.quote: As we talked about in our episode, in 2008, the company was on the brink of death. You had sold your headquarters building.

claims.claim: In 2014, print was the dominant engine of the business, but the company was getting its clocks cleaned by digitally native journalism companies.
claims.quote: Back then, print was still the lion's share; it was still the dominant engine of the business, and we were still doing great at the journalism. But I will say, we were getting our clocks cleaned by digitally native, upstart journalism companies at building a big audience for that journalism.

claims.claim: Netflix is the single entity controlling the media entertainment business today and has won, with no one ever going to beat them.
claims.quote: And Netflix, truly, if you say one, there's one entity that controls the media entertainment business today, and it is Netflix. They have won. No one is ever going to beat them.
